title: Outbreaks and transmission-based precautions
audience: Cleaners and cleaning supervisors working in residential aged care, clinics, dental practices and NDIS settings during an outbreak or under additional precautions, in any Australian state or territory.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: NHMRC, Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019) (no page date shown; document dated 2019); Aged Care Act 2024: news and commencement (no date shown).
learningOutcomes: Explain that an outbreak declaration or an additional precaution changes the instruction that governs cleaning, and that the cleaner follows the current formal instruction.
Identify the changes an outbreak instruction may make to entry, protection, product choice and cleaning frequency, and state who authorises each.
Recognise a conflict between a planned clean and a newly announced outbreak instruction, and state the stop-and-refer step.
Record the instruction followed, its effective time and any task postponed.

instruction.heading: What changes in an outbreak
instruction.body: An outbreak is a cluster of infections that the facility or public health authority has identified as a risk to residents, workers or visitors. When an outbreak is declared, the facility's infection prevention and control team may add precautions to the normal routine. These can include restricting entry to some areas, requiring particular protection, changing the products used, increasing the frequency of cleaning on specified surfaces, and using dedicated equipment. The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare set the national framework on which these facility decisions are based. The detail of what applies is set by the current formal instruction, not by a general memory of how outbreaks are managed.

instruction.heading: The governing instruction
instruction.body: The instruction that governs during an outbreak is the current formal instruction issued by the facility's clinical or IPC lead, usually in writing and posted in the area or sent to the supervisor. A verbal rumour, a message between colleagues, or a printed schedule that was prepared before the outbreak does not govern. If you hear that an outbreak has been declared and you have not received the formal instruction, ask your supervisor or the nurse in charge for it before starting the affected work. Confirm that the instruction is current and that it applies to the area you are about to clean.

instruction.heading: Entry, protection and dedicated equipment
instruction.body: Under an outbreak instruction, you may be asked to enter an area only after a particular step, to wear protection that is not part of routine work, or to use equipment that is dedicated to that area and not shared. Do not enter a restricted area without the instruction, do not substitute protection, and do not take equipment from the restricted area to a clean area. If the instruction requires you to wait outside until a clinical step is completed, wait, and record the time you waited and why.

instruction.heading: Products and frequency
instruction.body: Outbreak instructions may name a product, a dilution or a contact condition for a surface, and may require an increased frequency for specified high-touch surfaces. Use only the named product and the frequency in the instruction. If the named product is not available, do not substitute, and tell the supervisor so that the product is supplied. Do not increase the frequency beyond the instruction without written authority, and do not reduce it because the workload is high. Record each change in frequency or product as the instruction states it.

instruction.heading: Worked scenario: the planned clean and the outbreak briefing
instruction.body: A planned isolation-room clean overlaps with a newly announced outbreak briefing. The briefing may change the entry rules, the protection or the product for that room. The correct first step is not to enter the room until you have confirmed the current instruction with the clinical lead or IPC contact. If the instruction is not clear by the time you need to start, postpone the room, tell the supervisor, and record the time and the person you asked. Do not start the room on the assumption that nothing has changed.

procedure: On hearing of an outbreak or an additional precaution, obtain the current formal instruction from the clinical lead, IPC contact or supervisor before starting affected work.
Confirm the instruction is current, in writing, and applies to the area and the task.
Check the entry rules, the protection required, the products named and the frequency for each surface.
Postpone any task the instruction does not clearly permit, and do not start it on assumption.
Use dedicated equipment as the instruction requires, and keep it in the restricted area.
Record the instruction followed, who gave it, its effective time, and any task postponed, with the reason in plain terms.

workedExamples.situation: A colleague tells you an outbreak has been declared on the unit. Your schedule is unchanged and it lists a resident room for routine cleaning.
workedExamples.reasoning: Not until you have the current formal instruction. The rumour and the unchanged schedule do not govern. Ask the nurse in charge or the IPC contact for the instruction, and wait. If the instruction changes the room's entry, protection or product, follow it exactly. Record the time you asked and the instruction received.

workedExamples.situation: The outbreak instruction names a product for a handrail. The product on your trolley is a different one that you know works well.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you use the product on your trolley?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The instruction names the product, and a different product may not carry the required approval or contact condition. Do not substitute. Tell the supervisor so the named product is supplied, and postpone the handrail. Record the shortfall and the time.

equipmentAndPpe: Current formal outbreak instruction, held by the clinical lead or IPC contact
Dedicated equipment for restricted areas, as the instruction requires
Approved products named in the instruction: {{business:materials.approved_products}}

commonErrors.error: Starting a restricted area on the basis of a rumour or an unchanged schedule.
commonErrors.prevention: Obtain the current formal instruction in writing before starting affected work.

commonErrors.error: Using a familiar product that the outbreak instruction does not name.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only the named product. Report the shortfall and postpone the surface.

commonErrors.error: Carrying dedicated equipment from a restricted area into a clean area.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep dedicated equipment in the restricted area as the instruction directs.

commonErrors.error: Reducing the cleaning frequency because the workload is high.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the frequency in the instruction. Raise workload concerns with the supervisor.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019) provide the national framework for infection prevention and control in healthcare. The specific precautions for an outbreak are set by the facility's IPC team and the clinical lead under that framework.

Residential aged care operates under the Aged Care Act 2024, which commenced on 1 November 2025, and the facility's infection prevention procedures are its own obligation under the strengthened Aged Care Quality Standards.

Licence notice: Following an outbreak instruction does not grant any authority to make infection prevention decisions, declare an outbreak, or set precautions. This lesson does not grant any licence or authority.

qualityStandard: The learner states, for a supplied outbreak scenario, which instruction governs and how it is confirmed before work starts.
The learner applies a supplied outbreak instruction to entry, protection, product and frequency, and identifies the step each one changes.
The learner postpones a supplied task that the instruction does not clearly permit, and records the reason and the time.
The learner records the instruction followed, its source and its effective time.
documentationEvidence: The formal instruction followed, who gave it, and its effective time
Any task postponed, the reason in plain terms, and the person asked
Any product shortfall or dedicated equipment used, with the time
summary: An outbreak changes the governing instruction. Follow the current formal instruction, not a rumour or an old schedule.
Confirm entry rules, protection, products and frequency in writing before starting affected work.
Use only named products and dedicated equipment. Do not substitute or reduce frequency.
Postpone when the instruction is unclear, and record the instruction followed and the time.

knowledgeChecks.question: You hear that an outbreak has been declared, but you have not received a formal instruction. What should you do before starting a restricted area?
options: Start the area as scheduled, since nothing has been written down and the schedule is current
Start it, but use extra cleaning products to be safe, since the outbreak is only rumoured
Obtain the current formal instruction from the clinical lead or IPC contact before starting.

knowledgeChecks.question: An outbreak instruction names a product for a handrail. The product on your trolley is different. What should you do?
options: Do not substitute. Tell the supervisor so the named product is supplied, and postpone the handrail.
Use the product on the trolley, since it works well on handrails and is already in the room
Use half of each product to meet both requirements, so that the handrail gets both treatments

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these governs cleaning during an outbreak?
options: A verbal message between colleagues about the outbreak, passed on at handover
The current formal instruction issued by the facility's clinical or IPC lead.
The printed schedule prepared before the outbreak was declared.
